\chapter{Two Marks Inside a Verb}
\label{ch:bn-two-marks-inside-a-verb}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write the independent \bn{ও}, explain why a vowel following a vowel cannot be a sign, add the dot that turns \bn{য} into a glide, and read \bn{হওয়া} — the verb of being — straight off the page.}

The verb of being is read whole from four pieces bought in this chapter and the last, and set beside \bn{হ্যাঁ} to show that stacked pieces make one syllable and pieces in a row make several.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[o]{\bn{ও} — the independent o}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-o-indep}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{এ}}, then write \textbf{\bn{ো}} and say which letter it wraps around.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{ও}
\end{quote}

The fourth vowel this book has shown you in both of its bodies, and by now the arrangement should feel less like a rule and more like a habit:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{আ}} stands alone · \textbf{\bn{া}} rides a consonant
  \item \textbf{\bn{ই}} stands alone · \textbf{\bn{ি}} rides a consonant
  \item \textbf{\bn{এ}} stands alone · \textbf{\bn{ে}} rides a consonant
  \item \textbf{\bn{ও}} stands alone · \textbf{\bn{ো}} rides a consonant
\end{itemize}

The choice is never about the sound. It is about \textbf{whether the vowel has a consonant to sit on}. Opening a word, or following another vowel, it has none, so it needs a body of its own. That is the entire distinction, and it is the same distinction Devanagari, Gujarati and Telugu all make — one of the genuinely portable facts about the scripts of South Asia.

\textbf{\bn{ও}} is also a word in its own right, the everyday \emph{and} and \emph{also}, which is a convenience the other three vowels do not offer.

Say it long. The sign \textbf{\bn{ো}} and the letter \textbf{\bn{ও}} are the same \textbf{o} as in English \emph{go} — but without the slide toward \emph{w} that English adds. One steady vowel, not two.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হ}} + \textbf{\bn{ও}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{হও}}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{\bn{হ}} keeps its own inherent \textbf{ô}, and then \textbf{\bn{ও}} is a second syllable standing on its own feet. Two letters, two syllables — which is exactly why the vowel could not have been written as a sign here.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ও}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{আ} \bn{ই} \bn{এ} \bn{ও}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{হও}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{কেমন}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does a vowel need its standing-alone letter? (\textbf{When it has no consonant to ride} — opening a word, or after another vowel.) Do \textbf{\bn{ও}} and \textbf{\bn{ো}} sound different? (\textbf{No}.) And how many syllables are in \textbf{\bn{হও}}? (\textbf{Two}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(the dot below)]{\bn{়} — the dot below}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-nukta}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{য}} and say what it sounds like standing alone. Then read \textbf{\bn{হ্যাঁ}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{়}
\end{quote}

One dot, tucked under a letter. It adds no sound of its own. What it does is \textbf{change the letter it sits under into a different letter}, and Bengali uses it in exactly three places.

The one you need today:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{য}} + \textbf{\bn{়}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{য়}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{য}} on its own says \textbf{j}. With the dot it stops being a stop altogether and becomes a glide — the \emph{y} of \emph{yes} between vowels, and the \emph{w} of \emph{away} when the vowel beside it is round. It is the sound the letter used to have before Bengali hardened it, given back by a dot.

The other two are the same trick on another letter, and they are coming later in this book. What matters now is the shape of the idea: \textbf{Bengali did not invent new letters for these sounds. It marked old ones.} The dot is borrowed machinery — Persian scribes used it to bend Arabic letters into Persian sounds, and Indian scribes took the device rather than the letters.

Where the dot goes on the page is worth watching, too. It hangs below the body of the letter, the same country as \textbf{\bn{ু}}, and it is small. Two words can differ by this dot alone, so a reader who is skimming the head-line will read the wrong word rather than no word — the most expensive kind of mistake a script can offer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হ}} + \textbf{\bn{ও}} + \textbf{\bn{য়}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{হওয়}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{়}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{য} then \bn{য়}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jô} then \emph{yô} — stop, then glide
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{হওয়}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\bn{়}} add a sound? (\textbf{No} — it changes the letter above it.) What does \textbf{\bn{য}} become with it? (\textbf{A glide}, \emph{y} or \emph{w}.) And which mark sits \emph{above} the head-line rather than below? (\textbf{\bn{ঁ}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hôwā]{\bn{হওয়া} — to be, read whole}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-howa-read}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{য়}}. Then write \textbf{\bn{ও}} and say why it is not a sign.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হ}} + \textbf{\bn{ও}} + \textbf{\bn{য়}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{হওয়া}}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{হ}} — with its own inherent \textbf{ô}
  \item \textbf{\bn{ও}} — standing alone, because a vowel cannot ride a vowel
  \item \textbf{\bn{য়}} — the dotted glide, here doing the \emph{w} job
  \item \textbf{\bn{া}} — the vowel sign, on the glide
\end{itemize}

\textbf{hôwā} — \emph{to be, to become.} You met it romanized in the farewells chapter, as the verb hiding inside \emph{dækhā hôbe}, \textquotedblleft{}seeing will happen.\textquotedblright{} Here it is on the page, and every one of its four pieces was bought in the last two chapters.

Read it slowly and notice what is \emph{not} there. No stacked letters. No killed vowels. Four pieces in a row, left to right, each one saying its own thing. This is what Bengali looks like when a word is made mostly of vowels: the spelling stops being a puzzle and becomes a transcript.

Compare it with the word you read two chapters ago:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হ্যাঁ}} — five pieces, one syllable \textbf{\bn{হওয়া}} — four pieces, three syllables
\end{quote}

Same first letter, opposite arrangements. A Bengali reader's real skill is telling those two shapes apart at a glance, and it is a skill of the eye rather than the memory: stacked pieces are one syllable, pieces in a row are several.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{হওয়া}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{হওয়া}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hôwā} — three syllables, no cluster
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{হবে}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many syllables in \textbf{\bn{হওয়া}}? (\textbf{Three}.) Why is the \textbf{\bn{ও}} written standing alone? (\textbf{A vowel cannot ride a vowel}.) And what does the dot under the \textbf{\bn{য}} do? (\textbf{Turns it into a glide}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
